name: Fertilizer Injector Ratio Calculator
seoTitle: Fertilizer Injector Ratio Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Injector ratios tell you how much stock solution to mix so that the water reaching the plants carries the intended concentration. Free fertilizer injector rat
summary:
Injector ratios tell you how much stock solution to mix so that the water reaching the plants carries the intended concentration. It returns stock concentration, fertilizer per litre of stock and fertilizer per tank, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts between a target ppm in the irrigation line, the injector ratio and the weight of fertilizer for a stock tank of any size. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fertilizer Injector Ratio
sections.html:
Stock ppm = line ppm × injector ratio; grams per litre = stock ppm ÷ (%N × 10)

sections.title: How do I use the Fertilizer Injector Ratio?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: target nitrogen in the line of 150 ppm, nitrogen in the fertilizer of 20%, injector ratio of 100 :1, stock tank size of 200 L.

Substituting them into the formula gives stock concentration of 15,000 ppm, fertilizer per litre of stock of 0.0075 g/L, fertilizer per tank of 1.5 kg.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A 1:100 injector makes the stock 100 times stronger than the line, so a 150 ppm target needs 15 000 ppm in the tank.

  • Weigh fertilizers in grams per litre of stock, then check the electrical conductivity — it rises with concentration and is the quickest in-field check that the mix is right.

  • Nitrogen sources differ: calcium nitrate and ammonium nitrate carry different amounts of calcium and ammonium, which matters for pH drift in the root zone.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Confusing 1:100 with 1:99 — the difference is small for the stock strength but large for water accounting.
  • Mixing the stock in the irrigation line instead of the tank.
  • Using a fertilizer percentage as a decimal in one place and a percentage in another.

faq.q: How do I mix 100 ppm nitrogen with 20% fertilizer at 1:100?
Does the injector ratio affect the final EC?
faq.a: Yes: the line EC is set by the diluted concentration, so a stronger stock at a higher ratio can deliver the same EC.

faq.q: What does the Fertilizer Injector Ratio actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns stock concentration, fertilizer per litre of stock and fertilizer per tank. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
